title: Dedicated warm-capacity tradeoffs — decision brief
author: Asha Menon
content:
Summary
-------
This brief captures the decision rationale and implementation plan for the ‘warm capacity’ strategy for Redwood Dedicated customers. Warm capacity is defined here as kept-ready GPU allocations (partial or full instance reservations) that reduce cold-start and model-load latency at the expense of continuously incurred cost. The goal of this brief is to: (1) articulate tradeoffs between warm and purely burstable models, (2) provide concrete cost/latency models and thresholds for recommending warm allocations to customers, and (3) propose a phased rollout and observability requirements.

Context and motivation
----------------------
- Problem: Dedicated customers expect low tail latency for production LLM workloads (90–99.9th percentile) while also pushing to minimize monthly committed spend. When model weights are large and VM/GPU pre-warm time is non-trivial (30–300s), cold starts cause unacceptable user experience for interactive products.
- Existing behavior: We currently offer two extremes: fully reserved (always-on) Dedicated pools and burstable/shared-hosted fallbacks. There is a gap between cost-efficient burst strategies and SLA-safe always-on reservations.
- Goal: Define a middle path — warm capacity — with specific sizing and operational controls that balance latency SLOs and unit economics.

Decision summary
----------------
We recommend implementing a tiered warm-capacity model for Dedicated customers with three configurable knobs: (A) warm intensity (percent of peak reserved), (B) model preloading policy (full/partial/none), and (C) warm retention window (how long to keep allocated GPUs after last request). Default product behavior and recommended guardrails:
1. Default warm intensity = 30% of steady-state peak for newly onboarded Dedicated customers unless the customer requests otherwise.
2. Model preloading policy = partial (embeddings + first N layers cached) for large models (>25B) and full for small models (<=6B).
3. Warm retention default = 10 minutes; can be shortened to 60s for high-burst customers or extended up to 1 hour for high-interactivity SLAs.
Rationale: 30% warm intensity reduces high tail latency for the majority of short bursts while keeping additional committed cost within predictable bounds. Partial preloading reduces token-level latency impact without the full memory footprint cost of fully loaded replicas.

Quantitative tradeoffs and cost model
------------------------------------
Assumptions (example workload):
- Peak QPS: 100 requests/s, average session length 8 tokens per request average (interactive hooks), model = Redwood-Ref-13B
- Warm VM hourly cost (GPU + infra): $6.0/hour (example c5.GPU-like)
- Model load time (cold) = 180s; partial preload reduces first response by ~40%

Estimated monthly cost delta and latency gains (approximation):
| Option | Additional committed HW (%) | Monthly incremental cost per 100-peak-QPS | 95th-99.9th latency improvement |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| No warm (burst-only) | 0% | $0 | 95p: +150ms, 99.9p: +1.8s 
| 30% warm (recommended) | 30% | $1,296 | 95p: -80ms, 99.9p: -900ms 
| 60% warm | 60% | $2,592 | 95p: -150ms, 99.9p: -1.5s 
Notes: cost estimates assume 720 hours/month and single-GPU pricing; per-customer pricing will be applied to committed capacity SKU.

Alternatives considered
-----------------------
1. Always-on fully reserved pools: best latency but highest cost; recommended only for top-tier SLAs where latency SLOs require <50ms P95 and sustained throughput justifies commit.
2. Pure burst + pre-warmed cache on hosting fabric: minimizes committed spend but relies on cross-tenant warm cache that breaks isolation guarantees. Not acceptable for high-compliance customers.
3. Cold-start optimization microservices: faster model load via sharded weights + lazy init. Useful but does not eliminate large model cold-starts; treats symptom rather than economic tradeoff.

Risks and mitigations
---------------------
- Risk: Overprovisioning warm capacity increases customer bill shock and provisioning lead time. Mitigation: default conservative starter (30%), telemetry to provide per-customer cost projections before changes, and a UI preview for customers showing projected monthly delta.
- Risk: Warm instances consume scarce GPU capacity during cluster-wide spikes. Mitigation: cluster-level overflow policy (preemption priority tiers), and warm-intensity dynamic scaling during known surge windows.
- Risk: Partial preloading introduces additional runtime complexity and compatibility regressions. Mitigation: start with well-tested model families (Redwood-owned curated variants) and gate partial preloading by model profile.

Implementation plan (quartered rollout)
--------------------------------------
Phase 0 — Prototype (2 weeks)
- Implement warm-intensity config at scheduler level and partial preloading hook.
- Owner: eng-serving-runtime (lead: Priya Rao).
- Deliverable: internal canary with 3 internal tenants.

Phase 1 — Beta (6 weeks)
- Integrate billing projection UI in console and per-route SLO simulator.
- Add observability (per-tenant warm-usage, warm-hit-rate, warm-cost-estimate).
- Offer opt-in to existing Dedicated customers.

Phase 2 — Default opt-in (8 weeks)
- Default new Dedicated accounts to 30% warm.
- Expose retention window/service-level knob in account settings.
- Release developer-facing docs and runbook.

Phase 3 — Enterprise fine-tuning (ongoing)
- Introduce contract-level warm guarantees, SLAs, and dedicated support playbooks for warm-sizing negotiations.

Operational runbook (for SRE & CSM)
----------------------------------
- Typical alert conditions:
  - warm-utilization < 10% while warm-intensity >= 30% (indicates wasted commit)
  - warm-hit-rate < 50% with high tail latency (indicates mis-sized warm pools)
  - warm-preload-failure rate > 1% per hour (indicates runtime regressions)
- Runbook steps for each alert:
  1. Validate telemetry for the tenant (last 72h warm usage, request patterns).
  2. If utilization low, recommend warm reduction or toggle to burst for the tenant (CSM consult).
  3. If hit-rate low and latency high, increase warm retention or preload coverage for the affected model.
  4. For preload failures, roll model preloading back on the tenant and open a P1 incident if failures persist.
- Ownership: eng-sre owns alerting; customer-success/solutions owns customer conversations about resizing.

Console and API contract changes
--------------------------------
- New fields (Console & REST API):
  - warm_intensity_percent (integer)
  - warm_retention_seconds (integer)
  - preload_policy (enum: none, partial, full)
  - warm_cost_estimate (read-only string for UI)
Example API snippet (JSON):
{
  "tenant_id": "t-12345",
  "warm_intensity_percent": 30,
  "warm_retention_seconds": 600,
  "preload_policy": "partial"
}

Observability and SLOs
----------------------
- Required metrics (per-tenant): warm_allocated_gpus, warm_active_gpus, warm_hit_rate, cold_start_count, model_load_duration_seconds
- SLIs to track: P95 latency, P99.9 latency, cold_start_rate (per 10k requests)
- Initial alert thresholds:
  - cold_start_rate > 5 per 10k requests (investigate sizing)
  - P99.9 latency increase > 20% vs baseline after warm config change

Customer communication and pricing framing
---------------------------------------
- Pricing model: warm capacity is offered as a committed add-on SKU priced per-GPU/hour. For most customers, we will present a blended recommendation and show projected monthly delta in the console before any change.
- Suggested commercial behaviors:
  - Start customers at the conservative 30% default with a 30-day trial of warmed capacity for new enterprise accounts.
  - Offer an annual discount for customers who commit to warm percentages > 50%.

Success metrics (90 days after GA)
--------------------------------
- Reduction in tail-latency incidents attributable to cold starts by >= 70% for opted-in tenants.
- At least 60% of onboarding Dedicated customers accept the 30% warm default after seeing the projection.
- Warm-utilization > 35% across opted-in tenants (shows sensible sizing).

Open questions and follow-ups
----------------------------
- Should partial preloading be expressed as a model-specific tuning? (Action: product + applied-ml to define model profiles by 2026-04-01)
- How do warm guarantees interact with Dedicated autoscaling contracts and preemption semantics? (Action: SRE + legal to draft contract language by 2026-05-01)

Appendix A — Example math for console projection
------------------------------------------------
- Inputs: peak_qps, expected_warm_intensity, gpu_hourly_cost
- Projection: incremental_monthly_cost = warm_intensity * peak_capacity_in_gpus * gpu_hourly_cost * 24 * 30
- Example: peak_capacity_in_gpus = 10, warm_intensity = 0.3, gpu_hourly_cost = $6.0 -> 0.3 * 10 * 6 * 24 * 30 = $1,296/month

Appendix B — Backwards compatibility notes
-----------------------------------------
- Existing Dedicated API calls without warm_* fields will continue to behave as before (no warm allocation).
- Console will show a migration banner and estimate for each tenant recommended for warm.
